chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Two Ways Property Pays You

lessons.title: Why Residential Rental Yields in India Are So Low

children.text: In the last lesson, Priya's ₹80 lakh Wakad flat earned a gross rental yield of 3.3%. That was not a bad deal by Indian standards. It was a typical one. A ₹2.2 crore flat in Powai, Mumbai might rent for ₹60,000 a month. Park the same ₹2.2 crore in a bank FD and the interest alone would be higher, with no tenant, no society maintenance and no broker. So why do millions of Indians keep buying flats that pay less than a fixed deposit? By the end of this lesson you will know how low Indian residential yields really are, the five forces that keep them there, and what a low yield quietly assumes about the future.

body.text: Indian home prices are set by what buyers hope a flat will be worth tomorrow. Rents are set by what tenants can afford today. When hope runs far ahead of salaries, yield gets squeezed.

children.text: How Low Is Low?
Gross residential yields in large Indian cities generally sit between about 2% and 4%. Here is what that looks like across five micro-markets, using rounded, illustrative prices and rents.

body.caption: Illustrative gross rental yields in Indian micro-markets

children.text: Notice the pattern. Markets where tenants are mostly salaried IT employees, like Kondapur and Whitefield, sit at the higher end. Premium and luxury markets, where prices are driven by wealth rather than salaries, sit at the bottom. The more expensive the address, the lower the yield tends to be.

body.title: A Flat's Yield vs Other Indian Yields and Rates (%)

body.text: The chart uses approximate, rounded levels to show the gap, not live quotes. FD, G-sec and home loan rates move with RBI's repo rate, and REIT yields move with their unit prices on NSE and BSE. Check current rates before comparing a real property.

markDefs.definition: The annual loss you make when an asset's income is lower than the interest you pay on the money borrowed to buy it.

children.text: The most important gap in that chart is between the flat and the home loan. Borrow at 8% to own an asset yielding 3%, and every ₹1 lakh of loan costs ₹8,000 a year in interest while earning ₹3,000 in rent. That ₹5,000 difference is
negative carry
, and on a ₹70 lakh loan it adds up to ₹3.5 lakh a year before a single rupee of maintenance.
The Price-to-Rent Ratio: The Same Problem, Flipped

markDefs.definition: Property price divided by one year's rent. It tells you how many years of rent it takes to pay back the price.

children.text: Another way to see a low yield is the
price-to-rent ratio
. It works like a P/E ratio for property: instead of price divided by earnings, it is price divided by annual rent. A high ratio means you are paying many years of rent upfront.

body.caption: The two numbers are reciprocals: a higher price-to-rent ratio always means a lower yield.

children.text: The Powai flat costs ₹2.2 crore and earns ₹7.2 lakh a year, a price-to-rent ratio of about 31. In other words, a buyer pays roughly 31 years of today's rent upfront. The South Delhi builder floor, at ₹5 crore and ₹12 lakh a year, has a ratio of about 42.

body.title: Flip the ratio
body.textWithBlank: A flat with a price-to-rent ratio of 25 has a gross rental yield of ___%.
body.explanation: Gross yield = 100 ÷ 25 = 4%. You pay 25 years of rent upfront, so each year's rent is one twenty-fifth, or 4%, of the price.

children.text: Five Forces That Keep Indian Yields Low
Buyers pay for growth, not rent.

Most Indian property investors are buying the price they expect to sell at, not the rent. If a buyer believes a flat will rise 8% a year, a 3% yield feels acceptable, so the buyer bids the price up until the yield falls there.
Rents follow salaries, prices follow wealth.

A tenant can only pay what a monthly salary allows. A buyer can pay with accumulated savings, business profits, an inheritance, ESOP proceeds or NRI income. Prices can climb on that wealth for years while rents stay tied to take-home pay.
Holding an empty flat is cheap.

Municipal property tax in Indian cities is typically a small fraction of a flat's market value. With little cost to keeping a flat locked, many owners do not feel pressure to rent it out at all, let alone cut the rent to find a tenant.
Landlords have long feared tenants.

Decades of rent control made eviction slow and rents sticky. The 11-month rent agreement became standard partly to stay clear of tenant-protection laws and registration requirements. Fear of a tenant who will not leave keeps many owners out of the rental market, reducing how much rental income the housing stock generates.
Property is a savings habit.

For generations, land and flats were where Indian families stored wealth, alongside gold. Before demat accounts, SIPs and apps like Zerodha made financial assets easy to own, property was one of the few large, trusted places to park money. That demand has little to do with rent.

body.label: Vacant houses in urban India
body.context: Census 2011 counted roughly 1.1 crore vacant homes in urban India. Every one of them is a property earning a rental yield of zero.

body.title: A short history of rent control in India

children.text: Rent control laws were written to protect tenants during housing shortages. They did that, but they also froze rents in old buildings for decades and made landlords wary of letting property at all. Modern laws are trying to rebalance this, but adoption is slow because housing is a state subject.

content.title: Rent control and tenancy law in India

events.title: Bombay Rent Control Act
events.description: Rents in Bombay are frozen at old levels. Some tenants in old buildings in South Mumbai still pay rents of a few hundred rupees a month.

events.title: Delhi Rent Control Act
events.description: Strong tenant protections make eviction in Delhi slow and difficult.

events.title: Maharashtra Rent Control Act
events.description: Replaces the Bombay law, but older tenancies keep much of their protection.

events.title: Tamil Nadu tenancy law
events.description: Tamil Nadu passes a modern landlord-tenant law built on written agreements and a Rent Authority.

events.title: Model Tenancy Act approved
events.description: The Union Cabinet approves a model law with written agreements, a Rent Authority and a security deposit cap of two months' rent for homes. States must adopt their own versions.

body.title: What pushes yields up?
body.question: Which of these changes would RAISE the gross rental yield on flats in a city?
options: Prices fall 20% while rents stay the same
Rents stay flat while prices keep rising
More investors buy flats purely to hold for appreciation
Buyers start expecting 10% annual price growth
body.explanation: Yield is rent divided by price. If rent stays the same and price falls 20%, yield rises by a quarter: a 3% yield becomes 3.75%. The other three all push prices up relative to rent, which lowers yield.

children.text: What a Low Yield Silently Assumes

Nobody buys a 3% asset because they want 3%. When you accept a low yield, you are making an assumption about how much the price will rise. You can make that assumption visible with one line of arithmetic.

body.caption: A simple approximation. Chapter 4 replaces it with CAGR and XIRR on real cash flows.

body.title: The growth you are betting on
body.prompt: Arjun wants an 11% total annual return from a Kondapur flat. After maintenance and property tax, the flat's net rental yield is 2.5%. Roughly what annual price appreciation does Arjun need?
body.explanation: 11% − 2.5% = 8.5% a year. Sustained for ten years, 8.5% a year means the flat's price must rise to about 2.26 times its purchase price. That is the real bet behind a 2.5% net yield.

body.text: A low yield is not a fact about a property. It is a bet on its future price. When the bet pays off, nobody notices the yield. When it does not, as many NCR buyers found after 2014, a 2% to 3% yield leaves almost nothing to show for years of EMIs.

body.title: The Gurugram pitch
body.scenario: Vikram, an NRI working in Dubai, is pitched a ready 3BHK on Golf Course Extension Road, Gurugram for ₹3 crore. The broker says: "Rental income of ₹70,000 a month, prices here only go up." Vikram plans to put down ₹75 lakh and take a home loan of ₹2.25 crore at 8.5% for 20 years.
body.prompt: Work out the gross yield, the price-to-rent ratio and the size of the monthly gap. Then explain what this deal really depends on and what Vikram should check.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Gross yield: ₹70,000 × 12 = ₹8,40,000. ₹8,40,000 ÷ ₹3,00,00,000 × 100 = 2.8%.
2. Price-to-rent ratio: ₹3 crore ÷ ₹8.4 lakh ≈ 36. Vikram would be paying about 36 years of rent upfront.
3. The EMI on ₹2.25 crore at 8.5% for 20 years is about ₹1.95 lakh a month. Rent of ₹70,000 leaves a gap of about ₹1.25 lakh a month, or roughly ₹15 lakh a year, before maintenance, property tax, vacancy and tax on the rent. First-year interest alone is close to ₹19 lakh, more than double the rent.
4. The deal depends almost entirely on the second engine. Rent covers little, so the investment works only if prices rise strongly and a buyer is available when Vikram wants to sell.
5. Checks: actual registered resale prices in that sector over the last five years, not new launch prices; signed rents in the same society, not the broker's estimate; how much new supply is coming up nearby; and whether Vikram can fund a ₹1.25 lakh monthly gap for years without being forced to sell.
6. Compare the alternatives. A listed REIT or a debt fund could pay more than 2.8% with no loan, no tenant and daily liquidity.

body.title: When a low yield can be acceptable, and when it is a warning

columns.label: Can be acceptable
points: You have a long horizon and stable income to fund any gap
Jobs and infrastructure are already operating nearby, not just announced
You are buying with little or no loan
You plan to live in the property yourself later

columns.label: Warning sign
points: Yield is below about 2.5% and the loan is large
The growth story rests on projects that are only announced
Large unsold inventory in the same micro-market
You may need to sell within five years
The rent quoted is an estimate, not a signed agreement

body.title: Before you accept a low yield
steps: Collect signed rents for similar flats in the same society or lane, not asking rents from portals.
Calculate the gross yield and the price-to-rent ratio.
Compare the yield with your home loan rate to measure the negative carry.
Work out the annual appreciation you need to hit your target return.
Check that growth rate against actual resale prices in the micro-market over the last five to ten years.
Confirm you can fund the monthly gap for at least five years without being forced to sell.

cards.definition: Property price divided by annual rent. Gross yield equals 100 divided by this ratio.
The annual loss when an asset's income is lower than the interest on the loan used to buy it.
The annual price growth needed to reach a target return, roughly target return minus net yield.
Laws that limit rent increases and eviction. They protected tenants but made many landlords reluctant to let property.
A central model law with written agreements, a Rent Authority and a two-month deposit cap for homes, which states adopt individually.
Homes that are owned but not lived in or rented out, earning a yield of zero.

points: Gross residential yields in large Indian cities generally sit between about 2% and 4%, and premium markets sit at the lower end.
That is below FD rates, G-sec yields, listed REIT distributions and home loan rates.
Price-to-rent ratio is the flip side of yield: a ratio of 30 means a yield of about 3.3%.
Five forces keep yields low: buyers paying for growth, prices driven by wealth rather than salaries, cheap vacancy, landlords' fear of tenants, and property as a savings habit.
Borrowing at 8% to earn 3% creates negative carry that must be funded every month.
Every low yield hides an appreciation assumption. Calculate it: target return minus net yield.
Check that assumption against real resale prices before you buy.

Market rates and tenancy laws change and vary by state, so verify current figures and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser or a lawyer before making any decision.
